title: Karma yoga deep-dive: action as offering; Karma Yoga as taught by Vivekananda; work as worship (1 of 7)
hook: the first of three paths: what if the dishes were an offering?
tomorrow: Karma yoga deep-dive: action as offering; Karma Yoga as taught by Vivekananda; work as worship (2 of 7)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the silence after om, and the end of the Upanishads. The fourth: peaceful, auspicious, not two.

Four weeks in the depths of the Upanishads, and a fair question: fine, but I have a job. Kids, a commute, a sink full of dishes. When do I get to sit in the silence after om? The tradition's answer is a surprise: you don't have to leave the sink. Hindu teachers draw three great paths, three yogas, out of the Gita: karma, the path of action; bhakti, the path of devotion; and jnana, the path of knowledge. The next three weeks take them one at a time, starting with the one that begins at the sink.
screen: `I HAVE A JOB.` → `THREE PATHS.` → `THE ONE THAT STARTS AT THE SINK.`

segments.voice: Karma, from day seven, means action. Yoga means joining, yoking. Karma yoga is action that joins you to the divine instead of tying you up in knots. How? In chapter three of the Gita, Krishna says the world is bound by action, except action done as yajna: as sacrifice, as offering. Work done as an offering doesn't bind. Chapter nine makes it plain: whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer in worship, whatever you give, whatever discipline you keep, do it as an offering to me. Not only the rituals. The eating counts. The giving counts. The spreadsheet counts. So an offering isn't a special kind of act. It's a way of holding any act. You do it as well as you can, then let it go, into the hands of God, or of the whole, the way you'd set a flower down at a shrine and walk away without taking it back. The Isha made the same move at the start of the Upanishads: action that doesn't cling. Some Hindus say a word of offering before meals or before starting work, and some offer the fruits of the day at night. This week also brings Swami Vivekananda, the Hindu monk who taught in America and gave a set of talks in New York later published as Karma-Yoga. He'll put it bluntly, in his own way. But the root is this: offer the work.
screen: `KARMA: ACTION. YOGA: JOINING.` · `ACTION AS SACRIFICE DOESN'T BIND.` · `WHATEVER YOU DO, AS AN OFFERING.` · `SET IT DOWN, AND WALK AWAY.` · then, large: `OFFER THE WORK.`

segments.voice: Think of the next ordinary task on your list, and picture doing it carefully, the way you'd prepare something for someone you love. Then picture setting it down like a flower at a shrine and walking away, without looking back to see who noticed. If you pray, offer it silently to God as you understand God; if not, offer it to the people it will help, or to the day itself.
Karma yoga, action as offering. Whatever you do, eat, give or keep, done as an offering, doesn't bind.
Your line: offer the work. Any act can be held that way. A new path, on day two hundred sixty.

howItsDone: A common Hindu practice is to offer food before eating and to dedicate work to God, drawing on Gita 9.27; some end the day by offering its actions and their results at the family shrine.

original.note: Sanskrit: karma yoga, the yoga of action; karma from kri, to do; yoga from yuj, to join.

trapdoor: what you thought: karma yoga means doing good deeds to earn good karma.
what it means: it's any action done as an offering, without clinging to the result.
